title: Carbon Dioxide Removal
scope: Removing CO2 already in the atmosphere. Not solar geoengineering.
primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: a direct air capture unit as the dominant focal mass, a long low box whose face is a grid of large round fans; a pipe runs from its base down into a cut-away section of the ground, where it bends and descends through three wavy layers of rock strata to a small rounded pocket deep below; two round-crowned trees of medium size stand on the hill behind the unit, one overlapping its end; a few soft curved airflow lines drift across the whole sky toward the fans as the connective element; the ground is the gentle curve of a hill whose cut-away front shows the layers.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #3f9a6a, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: smokestacks, smoke, factories, oil derricks, flames, arrows, CO2 lettering or chemical formulas, globes, thermometers, melting ice, money, dollar signs, price tags, warning signs, protest signs.

overview.summary: Carbon removal pulls CO2 back out of the air. The central argument is whether relying on it adds to emission cuts or delays them.
overview.scope_covered: How much removal the world needs, what it costs, whether it works and can be verified, who pays, and whether relying on it helps or harms emission cuts.
overview.scope_excluded: Solar geoengineering, the pace of net zero, the phase-out of fossil fuels and carbon pricing in general, except where they bear on removal.
overview.why_now: The UN climate summit COP31 in Antalya closed on November 22, 2026 without adopting its main text. The draft had welcomed carbon dioxide removal with environmental safeguards and respect for Indigenous rights; at least 32 countries objected, partly because it did not respond to overshooting 1.5 °C.

stats.label: Carbon dioxide removed each year
stats.note: Human activity removes about 2.2 billion tonnes of CO2 from the air a year, 99.9 percent of it through forests, soils and wood products.
stats.detail: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal report, an independent assessment led by researchers at Oxford, the Mercator Research Institute, IIASA, the World Resources Institute and others, is the standard global count; it calls the total “equivalent to 5% of gross CO2 emissions.” The largest contributions come from China, the United States, the European Union, Brazil and Russia, and most of it is managed forests growing back. Fire, drought, pests or logging can reverse that storage. The figure counts only removal caused by deliberate human activity, not the much larger uptake by oceans and undisturbed land that would happen anyway. The forest figure is a ten-year average to 2023; the figures for newer methods run to 2025.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026)

stats.label: Removal pledges vs 1.5 °C scenarios
stats.note: Pledges add up to 3.6 billion tonnes of removal a year by 2050; the most ambitious 1.5 °C scenarios use 8.75 billion.
stats.detail: The report calls this the “CDR gap”: what governments have pledged, set against what modeled pathways that hold warming to 1.5 °C use alongside very fast emission cuts. The gap is 0.3 billion tonnes in 2030 and 1.2 billion in 2035. It has grown since the report’s previous edition because emissions kept rising, and the authors say it “will continue to widen without significant near-term action to reduce emissions.” Company announcements add up to over 5 billion tonnes a year in 2050, but the authors judge their credibility low. Only about a third of countries mention newer removal methods in their mid-century strategies. The scenario figures are model outputs, not forecasts: slower emission cuts raise the removal a pathway needs.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026)

stats.label: Carbon removal by novel methods each year
stats.note: Novel methods remove about 2 million tonnes of CO2 a year, a total growing about 40 percent a year.
stats.detail: The novel methods include biochar, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), direct air capture and enhanced weathering; biochar and BECCS account for almost all of the total. The report calls the growth rate similar to successful technologies like solar energy but “insufficient for the scale-up required to meet the Paris temperature goal.” Projects operating or under construction would reach 8 million tonnes a year of capacity in 2030, “although only 20% of planned capacity has been built in recent years.” In the most ambitious scenarios, removal by these methods grows fivefold between 2030 and 2035 and passes 3.5 billion tonnes a year by 2050.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026)

stats.label: Average price of removal credits by method, 2025
stats.note: Credits from direct air capture with storage sold for about US$593 a tonne on average in 2025; credits from forests sold for about US$17.
stats.detail: Prices span nearly two orders of magnitude, from US$1,301 for mineral products to the forest figure, and the spread broadly tracks durability: methods that lock carbon in rock or deep storage for thousands of years sell for hundreds of dollars a tonne, while forest credits that fire or logging can reverse sell for tens. The report cautions that price is not cost: sellers may price below cost with grant support or above it for margin, and prices for newer methods rest on few public data points. The average direct air capture price rose from US$315 in 2024. For comparison, the World Bank puts the average direct carbon price worldwide at about US$21 a tonne in 2026.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026), Table 4.3

stats.label: Remaining carbon budget for 1.5 °C
stats.note: From the start of 2026, about 130 billion tonnes of CO2 can still be emitted for 1.5 °C (central estimate), around three years at current emissions.
stats.detail: The annual Indicators of Global Climate Change update, led by Piers Forster with dozens of climate scientists, finds that human-induced warming reached 1.37 °C in 2025. Like any carbon budget, it shrinks by each year’s emissions. Once the budget is spent, bringing temperatures back toward 1.5 °C would require removing more CO2 than is emitted, which is why the budget runs through the argument over removal.
stats.source_label: Copernicus Climate Change Service, Indicators of Global Climate Change 2025

stats.label: Durable carbon removal delivered, of tonnes contracted
stats.note: Buyers have contracted about 50.5 million tonnes of durable carbon removal; as of November 2026 about 1.8 million, under 4 percent, had been delivered.
stats.detail: CDR.fyi tracks publicly reported purchases of durable removal, mostly forward contracts for tonnes to be delivered years from now, at an average price of about US$340 a tonne. Its June 2026 market update reported 30.4 million tonnes contracted in 2025 alone, after a 324 percent compound annual growth rate from 2021. The State of CDR report, using a different boundary, counts about 2 million tonnes delivered from newer methods by the end of 2025. Most contracted tonnes depend on plants that are not yet built.

stats.label: Microsoft’s share of durable carbon removal purchased
stats.note: Microsoft had bought about 78.5 percent of all disclosed durable carbon removal tonnes as of April 2026.
stats.detail: Buyers other than Microsoft and the Frontier coalition accounted for 17 percent of contracted tonnes but 90 percent of delivered ones, because they tend to buy smaller amounts for near-term delivery. The State of CDR report, on its own basis, finds Microsoft contracted 82 percent of novel removal tonnes in 2024 to 2025 and calls the concentration “a critical vulnerability for the ecosystem.” Microsoft has committed to be carbon negative by 2030; its 2026 environmental data fact sheet reports market-based emissions of about 21.1 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent in fiscal 2025, up from about 13.1 million in fiscal 2020, as it builds data centers for artificial intelligence. Bloomberg and Heatmap reported in April 2026 that it was pausing new deals; the company said its program “has not ended,” and in May 2026 it signed a 650,000-tonne deal with the biogas producer BioCirc (TechCrunch, 2026).

stats.label: Share of mitigation effort from carbon removal, most ambitious scenarios
stats.note: In the most ambitious scenarios, carbon removal does about 16 percent of the work of holding warming well below 2 °C; cutting emissions does the rest.
stats.detail: The report says limiting warming well below 2 °C “is achieved primarily through reducing sources of emissions,” with removal taking “an even stronger role” for 1.5 °C because those pathways must reach and sustain net-negative emissions. At the point net-zero CO2 is reached, removal balancing residual emissions comes to about 11 billion tonnes a year, five times today’s level. The report’s first system-level lesson is “prioritizing emissions reductions to limit CDR dependence.” Both sides of the debate cite the split: those building removal point to the size of its share in tonnes, those wary of it to the much larger share from cuts.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026)

stats.label: Annual growth needed for novel removal, against past technologies
stats.note: To reach the capacity companies have announced for 2030, novel removal would have to grow about 84 percent a year, faster than electric vehicles did.
stats.detail: The rates run from the tonnes delivered by the end of 2025 to the 42 million tonnes of capacity that 22 companies have announced for 2030, and to the capacity announced for 2050. The comparison rows are electric vehicles in use from 2005 to 2019 and solar photovoltaics from 1975 to 2018. The report also tests two proposed global 2030 goals: a “30 by 30” campaign for 30 million tonnes of novel capacity, which implies 57 percent annual growth, and the CDR2030 initiative launched at COP30, which aims for 100 million tonnes of novel and 3 billion tonnes of conventional capacity and implies 86 percent for novel methods. Against 181 historical technologies, the authors judge both ambitious but “not unprecedented”; lithium-ion batteries and internet traffic grew faster.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026)

stats.label: Estimated cost of direct air capture with storage
stats.note: A 2025 review puts direct air capture at US$400 to US$2,500 a tonne today and US$100 to US$600 at gigatonne scale; the IPCC’s 2022 range was US$100 to US$300.
stats.detail: The review, by van der Spek and colleagues and reported in the State of CDR, gives levelized costs of gross removal. The State of CDR says the wide range reflects different technologies and assumptions about energy, plant design and sorbents, and that many studies leave out compression, transport, storage and supporting infrastructure, so “more comprehensive cost assessments are, therefore, needed.” The US Department of Energy’s Carbon Negative Shot, removal for less than US$100 per net tonne by 2032, is a target, not an estimate.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026), citing van der Spek et al. (2025)

stats.label: Design capacity of the largest direct air capture plants
stats.note: Stratos in Texas is designed to capture 500,000 tonnes a year; Mammoth in Iceland, the largest operating plant, 36,000, though Heimildin reported it captured just over 100 in 2024.
stats.detail: Occidental says it will begin operating Stratos at the end of 2026, two years later than first expected; on its May 2026 earnings call it said testing of the first of the plant’s two units had found an issue with some components (E&E News, 2026). Climeworks opened Mammoth in 2024. The Icelandic outlet’s figure was reported by Latitude Media in June 2025, and in September 2026 Climeworks said sorbent and design upgrades had more than doubled Mammoth’s throughput and halved its operating cost per tonne, without giving tonnages (ESG Today, 2026). Design capacity is what a plant is built to do; delivered tonnes are what buyers pay for.

stats.label: Cumulative BECCS removal in IPCC 1.5 °C pathways, 2020 to 2100
stats.note: The IPCC’s 1.5 °C pathways use 30 to 780 billion tonnes of removal by bioenergy with carbon capture from 2020 to 2100, and 0 to 310 by direct air capture.
stats.detail: These are pathways that limit warming to 1.5 °C with no or limited overshoot. Net removal by agriculture, forestry and other land use spans 20 to 400 billion tonnes, and total cumulative net-negative CO2 emissions 20 to 660 billion. For 2 °C pathways the bioenergy range is 170 to 650 billion. The ranges are wide because the removal a model uses depends on its assumptions about cost, land and how fast emissions fall. The IPCC lists three roles for removal: lowering net emissions in the near term, balancing residual emissions from sectors such as agriculture, aviation, shipping and industry in the mid-term, and achieving net-negative emissions in the long term.
stats.source_label: IPCC AR6 WGIII Summary for Policymakers, paragraph C.3.5

stats.label: US 45Q tax credit per tonne of CO2 captured
stats.note: The US pays up to US$180 a tonne for CO2 captured from the air and up to US$85 at smokestacks and bioenergy plants, whether stored or used to recover oil.
stats.detail: The July 2025 budget law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, cut many clean energy credits but kept 45Q and raised the credit for using captured CO2, including to push more oil out of old fields, from US$130 and US$60 to match the credit for permanent storage. The full rate requires prevailing wages and apprenticeships, and facilities must begin construction before January 1, 2033. Treasury estimated the credit would cost US$36.2 billion over fiscal 2024 to 2033, and the Joint Committee on Taxation projects the 2025 expansion adds US$14.2 billion over fiscal 2025 to 2034, “driven largely by higher credit value for EOR.” Taxpayers for Common Sense, the fiscal watchdog that compiled these figures, argues the credit lacks verification and mostly rewards oil recovery; the Carbon Capture Coalition of companies, unions and environmental groups lobbies for it.
stats.source_label: Taxpayers for Common Sense, Section 45Q fact sheet (updated July 2025)

stats.label: Allowances the EU proposes adding to its carbon market to buy removals
stats.note: In July 2026 the European Commission proposed adding 250 million allowances to the EU carbon market for 2031 to 2040, spending the revenue only on certified permanent removals.
stats.detail: The revenue would go “exclusively to purchase BioCCS and DACCS certified under the Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming (CRCF) Regulation.” A further 10 million allowances would form a contingency reserve. Operators producing certified bioenergy removals at their own plants could use them against their own emissions, and removals stored in countries whose carbon markets are linked to the EU’s could qualify from 2031. The Commission presents the plan as giving industry breathing space and kickstarting the market. The EU’s scientific advisory board had recommended in February 2025 bringing permanent removals in only gradually, once certification is robust and if it does not deter emission cuts (Euronews, 2025). As of November 2026 the European Parliament and member governments had still to agree the text.
stats.source_label: International Carbon Action Partnership, EU ETS review proposal (July 2026)

stats.label: CO2 storage EU oil and gas producers must provide by 2030
stats.note: The EU requires 44 oil and gas producers to provide 50 million tonnes a year of CO2 injection capacity in geological storage by the end of 2030.
stats.detail: The obligation comes from Article 23 of the 2024 Net-Zero Industry Act, which sets a collective target and assigns shares to the oil and gas companies operating in the EU; the Commission named the producers on May 22, 2025. Storage is the shared bottleneck for carbon capture at factories and for durable removal such as BECCS and direct air capture. Producers have brought 15 legal cases against the provision at the EU courts, according to Bellona, which supports strict enforcement. Advocates of a carbon takeback obligation cite the rule as a working version of their idea, because it puts the cost of building storage on fossil fuel producers.
stats.source_label: European Commission, Directorate-General for Climate Action

stats.label: US direct air capture hubs funding paid out by mid-2026
stats.note: Of US$3.5 billion Congress set aside for direct air capture hubs in 2021, about US$31 million had been paid out by mid-2026.
stats.detail: The 2021 infrastructure law created the hubs as the world’s largest public program dedicated to removal demonstrations. The Department of Energy terminated 10 of its 21 awards in October 2025, revoking US$47 million for early-stage projects according to the State of CDR report. In April 2026 the department told Congress it was keeping the two large hubs, Occidental’s South Texas hub and Climeworks and Heirloom’s Project Cypress in Louisiana, each with US$50 million obligated against an original ceiling of up to US$600 million, while its 2027 budget request sought to rescind US$2.3 billion of the program (Heatmap, 2026). The analysis, by a former department official, finds neither hub had received new funds or contract changes in the months before July 2026.
stats.source_label: DOE Alumni Network, status of the Regional Direct Air Capture Hubs program (July 2026)

stats.label: Public research, development and demonstration funding for removal, worldwide
stats.note: Governments announced about US$5.4 billion of research, development and demonstration funding for carbon removal from 2019 to early 2026.
stats.detail: The total would be US$7.9 billion if the US direct air capture hubs program were fully funded. The report finds public funding spreading to new countries, including China and Saudi Arabia, while becoming unstable in the United States, and concluded in June 2026 that demonstration funding “currently depends less on technological readiness than on institutional continuity.” Removal is about 3 percent of all climate-technology funding. The largest long-term national commitment it records is Sweden’s BECCS support program, SKr 36 billion (about US$3.6 billion) over 2026 to 2046; Denmark has provided DKr 8 billion (about US$1.2 billion) to the Ørsted Kalundborg CO2 Hub. Private investment in removal companies rebounded to US$1.6 billion in 2025 after dips in 2023 and 2024, while climate-technology funding overall has fallen since 2022.
stats.source_label: The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd edition (2026)

stats.label: Canada’s federal commitment to buy carbon removal credits
stats.note: Canada has committed to buy at least C$10 million of permanent carbon removal credits by 2030, and on November 19, 2026 set up 19 standing offers to do so.
stats.detail: The government calls itself “the first national government to use competitive procurement for permanent CDR credits.” The offers cover five methods: direct air capture and storage, BECCS, biochar, other biomass carbon removal and storage, and enhanced mineralization; they run to March 31, 2029, extendable to March 31, 2031. The sum is small next to corporate buying, but government purchase is what the State of CDR report finds missing: it says “expectations of large and growing demand have become fragile” and that most policy supports supply rather than buying removal. The US Department of Energy’s CDR Purchase Pilot Prize, allocated US$45 million in 2026 according to the same report, is another government buying program.

questions.text: Does planning on carbon removal slow down emission cuts?
questions.why: If the promise of future removal lets governments and companies cut less today, removal could leave the climate worse off even if it works. Large-scale removal does not yet exist to test this, so the evidence on both sides is indirect.
questions.detail:
Those who see delay point to how models and targets have treated removal so far. Kevin Anderson and Glen Peters argued in Science in 2016 that the models behind the Paris goals assumed vast future removal, which made deep near-term cuts look unnecessary and passed the burden to later generations. Net-zero targets, which net removals against emissions, give every emitter a reason to promise removal later instead of cutting now. The largest buyer of removal has seen its own emissions rise since 2020, and once a removal industry exists it becomes a constituency for the emissions that feed it.

Those who see an addition answer that removal from newer methods is arriving in amounts far too small to excuse anyone, a sliver of annual emissions. Emissions are falling slowly for political and economic reasons that would exist without removal on offer, and the risk of crowding out cuts is a design problem that can be solved in how targets are written. And with the 1.5 °C budget nearly spent, removal will be needed to repair an overshoot either way.

questions.text: How much carbon removal will the world need?
questions.why: The answer depends on how fast emissions fall, how large the leftover emissions from farming, aviation, cement and steel turn out to be, and whether the world tries to bring temperatures back down after any overshoot of 1.5 °C.
questions.detail:
Those expecting billions of tonnes a year point to the scenario figures and to a carbon budget that will be spent within a few years, which makes any return toward 1.5 °C a matter of net-negative emissions for decades. Leftover emissions from agriculture and long-haul aviation have no full technical substitute in sight. Planning for too little removal and then needing more would be the costlier mistake, they argue, because removal industries take decades to build.

Those expecting far less note that the IPCC finds reliance on removal “significantly reduced” in pathways that assume more efficient resource use or a shift toward sustainable development. Each tonne not emitted is one that never has to be removed, at a fraction of the cost. Leftover emissions are not fixed: diets, materials efficiency, electrified industry and less flying shrink them. And the large removal numbers in models partly reflect assumptions that make future removal cheap, so they describe a modeling choice as much as a physical need.

questions.text: Can engineered removal become cheap and large enough to matter?
questions.why: Whether newer methods follow the learning curves of solar panels and batteries, or the stubborn costs of large one-off plants, decides whether billions of tonnes are affordable. Optimists cite early growth; skeptics cite physics and the first plants’ record.
questions.detail:
The optimistic case is that novel removal is growing at a pace similar to early solar, and the State of CDR report judges the growth needed for 2030 goals “not unprecedented” against 181 past technologies. Direct air capture plants are built from standardized modules, which get cheaper with repetition: Climeworks said in September 2026 that upgrades had more than doubled its Iceland plant’s throughput and cut its operating cost per tonne in half. A systematic review projects costs falling severalfold at gigatonne scale, and learning comes only from deployment, which early buyers are paying for now.

The skeptical case is that separating CO2 from air, where it makes up about 0.04 percent, takes a minimum amount of energy that no learning curve can remove, so direct air capture at gigatonne scale would need a large share of the world’s clean electricity. The flagship plants have delivered far less than their design capacity and run late. Cheaper methods such as BECCS, biochar and enhanced weathering are limited instead by biomass, land and the difficulty of measuring them.

questions.text: Should removals offset ongoing emissions, or be counted in separate targets?
questions.why: A tonne removed and a tonne not emitted have the same effect on the atmosphere, which argues for letting them trade. But a removal promised for later is less certain than an emission avoided today, and free trading is what critics fear will slow cuts.
questions.detail:
For offsetting: carbon markets work by finding the cheapest tonnes, and walling removal off from emissions raises the cost of climate goals and starves removal of the demand it needs to grow. A company or country that pays for a verified, permanent tonne of removal has done the same climate good as one that cut a tonne, and more than one that bought cheap avoided-emission credits. Corporate carbon-negative goals and plans to fund removal through carbon markets are how a market for removal gets built at all.

For separate targets: the EU’s scientific advisory board recommended in 2025 separate legally binding targets for gross emission cuts, permanent removals and temporary removals, because merging them sends the wrong signal to investors and lets cheap promises stand in for hard cuts. Separate targets let governments plan removal on its own merits while making sure emissions fall as fast as they can. Adding removal-backed allowances to a cap also loosens the cap today on the strength of removals delivered years later; if those removals fail, the emissions have already happened.

questions.text: Can carbon removal be measured and verified well enough to pay for?
questions.why: A buyer pays for a tonne nobody can see. Direct air capture with geological storage is metered at the plant and the well; weathering, ocean, soil and forest tonnes are estimated from models and sampling of open natural systems.
questions.detail:
Those who say it can be verified now point to fast-maturing rules: the EU adopted its Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming certification regulation, registries such as Puro.earth and Isometric publish methodologies and issue credits after third-party audits, and the IPCC is preparing a 2027 methodology report on counting removal in national inventories. Field trials and research networks for enhanced weathering add evidence each year, and conservative crediting, which discounts uncertain tonnes, lets buyers pay for what is known while science narrows the rest.

Those who say it is not yet reliable point to the voluntary carbon market’s earlier credibility collapse, after studies found that many forest offset credits did not represent real reductions, and see methods that model open systems facing the same risk at higher prices. For ocean methods the CO2 taken up can take months or years to equilibrate and is hard to trace; for enhanced weathering the share of rock that actually reacts depends on soil, climate and time. Paying hundreds of dollars a tonne for tonnes that cannot be confirmed invites a second scandal that would set the whole field back.

questions.text: Should carbon stored in trees and soils count the same as carbon stored in rock?
questions.why: Forests and soils supply almost all removal today, cheaply and with benefits for nature and livelihoods. But their carbon can return to the air through fire, drought or logging within decades, while fossil CO2 warms the climate for millennia.
questions.detail:
Those who would count all removal note that land-based removal is the only kind working at billion-tonne scale, available now while newer methods are in pilots, and that it pays communities and landowners to protect and restore ecosystems that matter for more than carbon. Refusing to count it would strip finance from forests, especially in the Global South, in favor of expensive machines in rich countries. Temporary storage still buys time while warming peaks, and buffers and monitoring can discount for the risk of reversal.

Those who would count only durable storage cite the IPCC: carbon in vegetation and soil “can be reversed by human or natural disturbances” and is “prone to climate change impacts,” while geological storage lasts 10,000 years or more. Myles Allen and colleagues argue for “geological net zero,” matching every tonne of fossil CO2 emitted with a tonne returned to permanent geological storage, because counting land sinks against fossil emissions would leave warming continuing at nominal net zero. The EU’s scientific advisory board warns that Europe’s own land sink is already declining under drought and fire.

questions.text: Who should pay for removing carbon from the air?
questions.why: Removal at billions of tonnes a year would cost hundreds of billions of dollars a year, and today one technology company and a few governments pay for most of it. Each way of paying carries a view of who is responsible.
questions.detail:
Public budgets treat removal as a public good, voluntary buyers treat it as corporate responsibility, carbon markets treat it as a compliance cost, and obligations on producers treat it as cleaning up a product.

Those who would have governments and committed buyers pay compare removal to flood defenses or vaccine stockpiles: early, expensive tonnes are a research investment that only they will make. Public procurement and advance market commitments, such as the Frontier coalition’s pledge of US$1.8 billion by 2040, give suppliers predictable demand without waiting for politically hard rules on fossil producers, and spreading the cost through budgets avoids raising household energy prices during the transition.

Those who would have fossil producers pay apply the polluter-pays principle: whoever extracts fossil carbon should pay to return it underground. Budgets and buyers have not produced steady demand: one company had bought about 78.5 percent of disclosed durable tonnes by April 2026, and US air capture hubs had received about US$31 million of US$3.5 billion by mid-2026. The EU’s storage duty on 44 producers shows such a rule can be legislated, and a cost producers carry passes into fuel prices, steering demand toward clean energy.

questions.text: Should fossil fuel companies be the ones building carbon removal?
questions.why: Oil and gas companies know how to drill wells, move gas by pipeline and manage reservoirs, which is most of what geological storage needs. They also have an interest in removal as a reason to keep selling oil and gas.
questions.detail:
Those who would use their skills note that storage underground is the bottleneck for every durable removal method, and that the people who have spent decades injecting fluids into rock are the ones who can do it safely and at scale. The EU’s storage obligation on oil and gas producers rests on the same logic: they already have the subsurface data, wells and know-how. Excluding them would slow removal for reasons of image rather than climate, since a tonne taken from the air counts the same whoever takes it.

Those who would keep them out quote Occidental’s then chief executive Vicki Hollub, who said in 2022, “If we focus on emissions, I think there is a way to continue the production of oil and gas for the foreseeable future,” the opposite of what removal is for in climate pathways. Captured CO2 can be injected to squeeze more oil from depleted reservoirs, and the US tax credit pays the same for that as for permanent storage. A removal industry led by fossil producers, on this view, has every incentive to promise removal and slow the phase-out of the fuels that make it necessary.

positions.name: Scale up carbon removal now, alongside deep emission cuts
positions.steelman: Removal is the part of the climate job that cutting emissions cannot do, and an industry that has to reach billions of tonnes must start being built now.
positions.detail:
The IPCC finds removal “unavoidable” for balancing the residual emissions that are hardest to cut, and with the 1.5 °C budget nearly gone it is also the only way to bring temperatures back down after an overshoot. Billions of tonnes a year cannot be switched on in 2045. Solar, wind and batteries took decades of early, expensive deployment to become cheap, and removal needs the same runway, starting now: forests and soils today, biochar and BECCS next, direct air capture and weathering as they mature, with strict measurement and permanent storage for the tonnes that balance fossil emissions. The bottleneck is demand, not technology. When one company buys most of the world’s durable removal, governments have to become buyers too, through procurement and compliance markets.

Removal is never a substitute for cutting emissions, and the risk that it delays cuts is real; that is why we back separate targets, limits on how much removal counts, and rules that only permanent removal can balance fossil CO2. But the alternative to building removal is not faster cuts. It is reaching mid-century with residual emissions, an overshoot and no tools to answer them. We differ among ourselves on whether removal should trade in carbon markets now or wait for proven certification, and on how much weight land-based methods deserve against engineered ones.

positions.name: Cut emissions instead of relying on engineered removal
positions.steelman: The only sure way to stop warming is to stop burning fossil fuels, and every promise of future removal becomes an excuse to keep emitting today.
positions.detail:
Engineered removal has been promised for decades and has delivered almost nothing: a few million tonnes a year from newer methods, about a hundred tonnes in 2024 from the flagship direct air capture plant, a small fraction of contracted tonnes delivered, and most of the CO2 captured in the United States sent to pump more oil. The fossil fuel industry knows what removal is worth to it, which is why the Center for International Environmental Law counted a record 700 carbon capture lobbyists at COP31, and why producers champion capture and removal while expanding production. Money spent at several hundred dollars a tonne on machines is money not spent on renewables, efficiency and electrification. The IPCC itself warns that biomass crops for BECCS, “when poorly implemented,” can harm biodiversity, food and water security and “the rights of Indigenous Peoples, especially if implemented at large scales and where land tenure is insecure.”

The IPCC calls removal unavoidable only to balance leftover emissions after deep cuts, and how large those leftovers are is a choice. The honest response to overshoot is to cut faster, not to bet the future on technologies that have not worked at scale. Some of us reject all removal markets, forest offsets included, as false solutions; others accept ecosystem restoration and limited research into new methods but oppose subsidies and any reliance on removal in targets. Protecting forests, wetlands and the land rights of the people who live there is worth doing for its own sake, never as credits that let polluters keep polluting.
positions.proponents: Center for International Environmental Law; Kevin Anderson; Biofuelwatch

positions.name: Keep oil and gas and capture or remove their carbon
positions.steelman: The problem is the emissions, not the oil and gas, and the world will use both for decades, so capture the carbon and remove what cannot be captured.
positions.detail:
Demand for oil and gas keeps growing in developing economies, and nothing else yet matches them for scale, reliability and price. The fastest realistic route to net zero is to capture emissions where they are made and pull from the air what cannot be captured. Our industry has the geologists, wells, pipelines, reservoirs and capital, has injected CO2 underground since the 1970s, and is building the world’s largest direct air capture plant. Congress, under majorities of both parties, has extended or expanded the US credit for captured carbon in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2025. Forcing an early end to fossil fuels would raise energy costs, weaken energy security and push production toward less careful producers. As OPEC’s Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais wrote in 2024, the industry is “showing that it is possible to reduce emissions while producing the oil the world needs.”

To the charge that this is a license to keep polluting: a tonne captured or removed and stored is a tonne out of the atmosphere, whoever does it and whatever else they sell. Those who want fossil fuels phased out have no plan for the demand that remains meanwhile, and shutting producers out of capture means it is met with nothing captured. Nor is it a free ride: Occidental has sunk its own capital into its plant and has said it cannot keep investing without regulators and buyers. Producers differ in how far they go, from Occidental’s direct air capture business to Saudi Arabia’s circular carbon economy of reducing, reusing, recycling and removing carbon.
positions.proponents: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries; Occidental Petroleum; Government of Saudi Arabia

positions.name: Require fossil fuel producers to store the carbon they sell
positions.steelman: Warming stops when every tonne of fossil carbon taken out of the ground is put back, so the companies that sell it should be made to store it.
positions.detail:
The debate is stuck between those who want removal paid for by taxpayers and a few technology companies and those who want no removal at all, and neither will stop warming. Require producers and importers to store a rising share of the CO2 from what they sell, reaching 100 percent by the net-zero year, and storage and removal get built at the pace and scale needed, paid for by the polluter rather than the public. The cost passes gradually into fuel prices, which steers demand toward clean energy without a sudden shock. Only permanent geological storage should count against fossil emissions. The EU has already shown such a rule can be written into law and that it bites: its storage requirement on oil and gas producers has drawn legal challenges from the producers themselves.

To those who say an obligation legitimizes extraction, we answer that it does the opposite. A rising storage requirement raises the cost of every barrel and tonne of fossil fuel year after year, until extraction without matching storage is impossible, which phases out unabated fossil fuels through price rather than decree. Myles Allen of Oxford, a lead author of an August 2026 open letter urging the UK to make such an obligation a condition of approving new extraction, put it plainly: “This is not a ‘get-out-of-jail-free card’ for the fossil fuel industry.” We differ on whether to set the obligation nationally or across a bloc like the EU, whether it should cover only new extraction or all fossil carbon sold, and how fast the stored share should rise.
positions.proponents: Myles Allen; Carbon Balance Initiative; Bellona Europa; Stephanie Loo

crux.lead: Does relying on carbon removal add to emission cuts, or replace them?
crux.lead_highlight: add to emission cuts, or replace them
crux.subtitle: All camps agree warming stops only when the CO2 emitted is balanced by CO2 removed. They split over whether counting on removal brings that balance closer or lets emitters put off cuts.
crux.empirical: Two things can be tested: whether removal arrives at the scale, cost and permanence plans assume, as contracted tonnes come due and methods used in fields and oceans prove measurable or not, and whether those who plan on removal cut emissions faster or slower than others.
crux.values: No data says how much risk of failure it is fair to pass to later generations, or whether continued fossil emissions may rightly be balanced by removal at all. One side fears leftover emissions with no way to take them back; the other, a promise of removal that fails.
